claim: Inhomogeneous diffusivity has been identified as a ubiquitous feature of the cellular interior.
source: While inhomogeneous diffusivity has been identified as a ubiquitous feature of the cellular interior, its implications for particle mobility and concentration at different length scales remain largely unexplored.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research establishing heterogeneous diffusivity in cells.

claim: The implications of inhomogeneous diffusivity for particle mobility and concentration at different length scales remain largely unexplored.
source: While inhomogeneous diffusivity has been identified as a ubiquitous feature of the cellular interior, its implications for particle mobility and concentration at different length scales remain largely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Diffusive lensing is a nonequilibrium mode of membrane-less compartmentalization arising from the convergence of diffusive trajectories into low-diffusive sinks.
source: We propose that a nonequilibrium mode of membrane-less compartmentalization arising from the convergence of diffusive trajectories into low-diffusive sinks, which we call 'diffusive lensing,' is relevant for living systems.
evidence: This is the main theoretical proposal of the work, supported by the simulations presented.

claim: Diffusive lensing is relevant for living systems.
source: We propose that a nonequilibrium mode of membrane-less compartmentalization arising from the convergence of diffusive trajectories into low-diffusive sinks, which we call 'diffusive lensing,' is relevant for living systems.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the modeling results and biological context.

claim: Diffusive lensing is a potentially key driver of mesoscale dynamics in the cytoplasm.
source: Our work highlights the phenomenon of diffusive lensing as a potentially key driver of mesoscale dynamics in the cytoplasm, with possible far-reaching implications for biochemical processes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the simulation results.

claim: Diffusive lensing has possible far-reaching implications for biochemical processes.
source: Our work highlights the phenomenon of diffusive lensing as a potentially key driver of mesoscale dynamics in the cytoplasm, with possible far-reaching implications for biochemical processes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential implications.

claim: Diffusion of individual components in cells occurs in a complex, crowded milieu.
source: In cells, diffusion of individual components occurs in a complex, crowded milieu (Ellis, 2001; Luby-Phelps, 1999; van den Berg et al., 2017) that is known to exhibit position-dependent diffusivity (Berret, 2016; Garner et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2020; Śmigiel et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The cellular milieu is known to exhibit position-dependent diffusivity.
source: In cells, diffusion of individual components occurs in a complex, crowded milieu (Ellis, 2001; Luby-Phelps, 1999; van den Berg et al., 2017) that is known to exhibit position-dependent diffusivity (Berret, 2016; Garner et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2020; Śmigiel et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent research.

claim: Diffusivity varies inversely with viscosity.
source: Diffusivity varies inversely with viscosity, a key biophysical parameter of the cytoplasm (Bausch et al., 1999; Hu et al., 2017) that dictates translational and rotational mobility of proteins and, by extension, possibly influences their activity (Huang et al., 2022; Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 2001; Pan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established physical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Viscosity is a key biophysical parameter of the cytoplasm that dictates translational and rotational mobility of proteins.
source: Diffusivity varies inversely with viscosity, a key biophysical parameter of the cytoplasm (Bausch et al., 1999; Hu et al., 2017) that dictates translational and rotational mobility of proteins and, by extension, possibly influences their activity (Huang et al., 2022; Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 2001; Pan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Viscosity possibly influences protein activity.
source: Diffusivity varies inversely with viscosity, a key biophysical parameter of the cytoplasm (Bausch et al., 1999; Hu et al., 2017) that dictates translational and rotational mobility of proteins and, by extension, possibly influences their activity (Huang et al., 2022; Lippincott-Schwartz et al., 2001; Pan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations.

claim: Diffusivity has been implicated in modulating or driving a range of cellular processes.
source: While diffusivity has been implicated in modulating or driving a range of cellular processes (Molines et al., 2022; Persson et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022), the role of inhomogeneous diffusivity in shaping biochemistry by regulating biomolecular concentration and dynamics remains poorly understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The role of inhomogeneous diffusivity in shaping biochemistry by regulating biomolecular concentration and dynamics remains poorly understood.
source: While diffusivity has been implicated in modulating or driving a range of cellular processes (Molines et al., 2022; Persson et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022), the role of inhomogeneous diffusivity in shaping biochemistry by regulating biomolecular concentration and dynamics remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The accumulation of small molecules within the nuclear pore has been attributed to diffusion through a viscous region.
source: The accumulation of small molecules within the nuclear pore, for instance, has been attributed to diffusion through a viscous region (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Chladni patterns are an example of particle concentration resulting from inhomogeneous stochastic transport coefficients.
source: At the macroscale, Chladni patterns are an example of particle concentration resulting from inhomogeneous stochastic transport coefficients (Grabec, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The implications of inhomogeneous diffusivity as a nonequilibrium phenomenon occurring at time scales and length scales relevant to biology remain largely unexplored.
source: The implications of inhomogeneous diffusivity as a nonequilibrium phenomenon occurring at time scales and length scales relevant to biology remain largely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: More information is required to specify the problem of inhomogeneous diffusion than just the diffusion constant.
source: Theoretically, more information is required to specify the problem than just the diffusion constant: different mathematical interpretations of the stochastic term in diffusion equations with a spatially inhomogeneous diffusion constant result in different physical predictions (see Appendix for more information).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the mathematical modeling of diffusion.

claim: Different mathematical interpretations of the stochastic term in diffusion equations with a spatially inhomogeneous diffusion constant result in different physical predictions.
source: Theoretically, more information is required to specify the problem than just the diffusion constant: different mathematical interpretations of the stochastic term in diffusion equations with a spatially inhomogeneous diffusion constant result in different physical predictions (see Appendix for more information).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about mathematical modeling.

claim: Particles accumulated in the low-diffusivity zone in simulations with a step-like lower-diffusivity region.
source: Over the course of the simulation, particles accumulated in the low-diffusivity zone (Figure 1A and C), consistent with steady-state closed form Itô-convention solutions (Tupper and Yang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: Particle accumulation in low-diffusivity zones is consistent with steady-state closed form Itô-convention solutions.
source: Over the course of the simulation, particles accumulated in the low-diffusivity zone (Figure 1A and C), consistent with steady-state closed form Itô-convention solutions (Tupper and Yang, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with theoretical predictions from cited work.

claim: Similar accumulation was observed in a smooth diffusivity gradient.
source: A similar accumulation was observed in a smooth diffusivity gradient (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1B and D.

claim: Agent-based simulations demonstrate that under the Itô convention, areas of decreased diffusivity lead to increases in the concentration of diffusing particles.
source: Thus, agent-based simulations demonstrate that under the Itô convention, areas of decreased diffusivity lead to increases in the concentration of diffusing particles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results presented.

claim: At low interaction strength, clustering occurred only at the low-diffusivity end of a gradient.
source: At low interaction strength, clustering occurred only at the low-diffusivity end of a gradient (Figure 2A), while the same interaction strength was insufficient to produce clusters in a uniform diffusivity distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: The same low interaction strength was insufficient to produce clusters in a uniform diffusivity distribution.
source: At low interaction strength, clustering occurred only at the low-diffusivity end of a gradient (Figure 2A), while the same interaction strength was insufficient to produce clusters in a uniform diffusivity distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: At high interaction strength, robust clustering manifested before particle gradient formation reached the steady-state, leading to clustering towards the high-diffusivity side of the simulation region as well.
source: In contrast, a high interaction strength resulted in robust clustering manifesting before particle gradient formation reached the steady-state, leading to clustering towards the high-diffusivity side of the simulation region as well (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At high interaction strength, the clustering rate remained the same throughout the region in the absence of a gradient.
source: At this high interaction strength, the clustering rate remained the same throughout the region in the absence of a gradient (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and D.

claim: Diffusive lensing can modulate clustering and under certain circumstances cause diffusivity-dependent localized cluster formation.
source: Taken together, the results reveal that diffusive lensing can modulate clustering and under certain circumstances cause diffusivity-dependent localized cluster formation, and furthermore that the relative strengths and timescales of each phenomenon quantitatively dictate whether increased clustering will preferentially occur in low-diffusive zones.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the simulation results presented.

claim: The relative strengths and timescales of diffusive lensing and inter-particle interactions quantitatively dictate whether increased clustering will preferentially occur in low-diffusive zones.
source: Taken together, the results reveal that diffusive lensing can modulate clustering and under certain circumstances cause diffusivity-dependent localized cluster formation, and furthermore that the relative strengths and timescales of each phenomenon quantitatively dictate whether increased clustering will preferentially occur in low-diffusive zones.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the simulation results presented.

claim: Particle diffusion was unencumbered in the case of large bounds relative to step size.
source: Particle diffusion was unencumbered in the case of large bounds (relative to step size) (Figure 3A) and confined in the case of small bounds (Figure 3B) all in agreement with earlier results (Dix and Verkman, 2008; Saxton, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior research.

claim: Particle diffusion was confined in the case of small bounds.
source: Particle diffusion was unencumbered in the case of large bounds (relative to step size) (Figure 3A) and confined in the case of small bounds (Figure 3B) all in agreement with earlier results (Dix and Verkman, 2008; Saxton, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior research.

claim: The MSD at saturation in homogeneously diffusive systems was found to be agnostic to the underlying uniform diffusivity of the system.
source: The MSD at saturation in homogeneously diffusive systems was found to be agnostic to the underlying uniform diffusivity of the system, indicating that it is exclusively determined by the simulation region size.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of simulation data.

claim: The saturation MSD in homogeneously diffusive systems is exclusively determined by the simulation region size.
source: The MSD at saturation in homogeneously diffusive systems was found to be agnostic to the underlying uniform diffusivity of the system, indicating that it is exclusively determined by the simulation region size.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Particles in a diffusivity gradient exhibited dynamics intermediate to those of homogeneous high and low diffusivity cases, both in the diffusion coefficient and saturation MSD.
source: In contrast, particles in a diffusivity gradient exhibited dynamics intermediate to those of homogeneous high and low diffusivity cases, both in the diffusion coefficient and saturation MSD (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The lowering of the saturation MSD reflects particle diffusion occurring within apparent simulation region bounds that confine more than the actual simulation region size.
source: The lowering of the saturation MSD reflects particle diffusion occurring within apparent simulation region bounds that confine more than the actual simulation region size.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: For most of the diffusivity ratio parameter space, irrespective of whether the smaller zones were more or less diffusive relative to the bulk, a reduction in MSD was seen indicating effectively lower diffusion bounds.
source: For most of the diffusivity ratio parameter space, irrespective of whether the smaller zones were more or less diffusive relative to the bulk, a reduction in MSD was seen indicating effectively lower diffusion bounds (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The saturation MSD was found to depend on the location of the low-diffusive zone.
source: The saturation MSD was also found to depend on the location of the low-diffusive zone: a more-centered zone resulted in a lowered saturation value, possibly due to weaker ratchet effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: A more-centered low-diffusive zone resulted in a lowered saturation MSD value, possibly due to weaker ratchet effects.
source: The saturation MSD was also found to depend on the location of the low-diffusive zone: a more-centered zone resulted in a lowered saturation value, possibly due to weaker ratchet effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data and includes a speculative explanation.

claim: These results point to the insufficiency of using the diffusion coefficient alone to describe diffusion in heterogenous milieu.
source: These results point to the insufficiency of using the diffusion coefficient alone to describe diffusion in heterogenous milieu.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The decrease in average mobility arose from changes in flux between the low-diffusive and bulk zones, as reflected by an increase in mean dwell times of particles within low-diffusive granules.
source: The decrease in average mobility in all three cases arose from changes in flux between the low-diffusive and bulk zones, as reflected by an increase in mean dwell times of particles within low-diffusive granules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G and H.

claim: Averaging the granular and bulk diffusivity values to produce weighted-average diffusivity values resulted in slower dynamics than that of the equivalent granule-comprising simulations.
source: Such an averaging of the diffusivity to cause an effective uniform mobility for all resident particles resulted in slower dynamics than that of the equivalent granule-comprising simulations (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhomogeneity in diffusivity drives rapid effective dynamics via fluxes between the granular (interior) and bulk (exterior) environments, creating 'diffusive highways' for particles to move rapidly between low-diffusive regions.
source: We conclude that inhomogeneity in diffusivity drives rapid effective dynamics via fluxes between the granular (interior) and bulk (exterior) environments, creating 'diffusive highways' for particles to move rapidly between low-diffusive regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The diffusive lensing of particles into low-diffusive zones, and their consequent dwelling in these regions, can be tuned by modulating the underlying diffusivity distribution in myriad ways.
source: The diffusive lensing of particles into low-diffusive zones, and their consequent dwelling in these regions, can be tuned by modulating the underlying diffusivity distribution in myriad ways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The complex milieu of the cellular interior has been recently shown to feature heterogeneous diffusivity.
source: The complex milieu of the cellular interior has been recently shown to feature heterogeneous diffusivity (Garner et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2020; Parry et al., 2014; Śmigiel et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2020), yet the consequences of such inhomogeneity on compartmentalization and mesoscale molecular dynamics have remained unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent research.

claim: The consequences of heterogeneous diffusivity on compartmentalization and mesoscale molecular dynamics have remained unclear.
source: The complex milieu of the cellular interior has been recently shown to feature heterogeneous diffusivity (Garner et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2022; McLaughlin et al., 2020; Parry et al., 2014; Śmigiel et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2020), yet the consequences of such inhomogeneity on compartmentalization and mesoscale molecular dynamics have remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Through agent-based modeling of diffusion using the Itô integration convention, heterogenous diffusivity can lead to simulated particle trajectories converging into low-diffusive hotspots, causing the accumulation of diffusing particles into membrane-less compartments defined by the lower-diffusivity zones.
source: Through agent-based modeling of diffusion using the Itô integration convention, we show that heterogenous diffusivity can lead to simulated particle trajectories converging into low-diffusive hotspots, causing the accumulation of diffusing particles into membrane-less compartments defined by the lower-diffusivity zones.
evidence: This is the main finding of the work, supported by simulation data.

claim: The underlying conclusions from the 2D simulations extend to 3D directly.
source: The underlying conclusions from our 2D simulations extend to 3D directly (see Methods).
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the results.

claim: Diffusive lensing can occur across a wide parameter space.
source: Diffusive lensing has wide-ranging effects on particle distribution and dynamics and, furthermore, it can occur across a wide parameter space.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Diffusive lensing is a ubiquitous phenomenon in living systems.
source: We, therefore, speculate that diffusive lensing is a ubiquitous phenomenon in living systems.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Inhomogeneous diffusivity allows for particle mobility at the microscale and mesoscale to be different from that expected in the presence of homogeneous diffusion.
source: We found that inhomogeneous diffusivity allows for particle mobility at the microscale and mesoscale to be different from that expected in the presence of homogeneous diffusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Such an expectation of different mobility is in line with predicted and observed deviations from normal diffusion in cells.
source: Such an expectation is in line with predicted and observed deviations from normal diffusion in cells (Bancaud et al., 2012; Baum et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The relative strengths of diffusive lensing and inter-particle interactions determined the extent to which clustering was modulated by diffusive lensing.
source: The relative strengths of diffusive lensing and inter-particle interactions (if any) determined the extent to which clustering was modulated by diffusive lensing: this interplay may be important for determining the effects of inhomogeneous diffusivity on biochemical reaction rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The interplay between diffusive lensing and inter-particle interactions may be important for determining the effects of inhomogeneous diffusivity on biochemical reaction rates.
source: The relative strengths of diffusive lensing and inter-particle interactions (if any) determined the extent to which clustering was modulated by diffusive lensing: this interplay may be important for determining the effects of inhomogeneous diffusivity on biochemical reaction rates.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential implications.

claim: In the case that particle concentration decreases diffusivity, diffusive lensing may create a positive feedback loop that drives particles into areas where low diffusivity has been nucleated.
source: In the case that particle concentration decreases diffusivity (for example in the case of branched polysaccharides like glycogen), diffusive lensing may create a positive feedback loop that drives particles into areas where low diffusivity has been nucleated.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a potential mechanism.

claim: Spatially-averaged effective diffusion timescales were found to depend on the microscopic diffusivity distribution.
source: Spatially-averaged effective diffusion timescales were found to depend on the microscopic diffusivity distribution: the same average diffusivity can give rise to slower or faster dynamics depending on whether it is realized via homogeneous or heterogenous diffusivity distributions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The same average diffusivity can give rise to slower or faster dynamics depending on whether it is realized via homogeneous or heterogenous diffusivity distributions.
source: Spatially-averaged effective diffusion timescales were found to depend on the microscopic diffusivity distribution: the same average diffusivity can give rise to slower or faster dynamics depending on whether it is realized via homogeneous or heterogenous diffusivity distributions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: The bulk region interspersed between the low-diffusive hotspots provides 'diffusive highways' that contribute to large fluxes at the diffusivity interface, thereby accounting for the faster dynamics.
source: In the latter case, the bulk region interspersed between the low-diffusive hotspots provides 'diffusive highways' that contribute to large fluxes at the diffusivity interface, thereby accounting for the faster dynamics.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: Such expressways and their associated fluxes may impact reaction kinetics by altering substrate turnover rates.
source: Such expressways and their associated fluxes may impact reaction kinetics by altering substrate turnover rates, congruent with the model of unusual transport processes potentially modifying reaction kinetics (Bénichou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation.

claim: Cells may compensate for geometry-imposed constraints on packing density and size of low-diffusive regions by altering the diffusivity ratio against the bulk milieu instead.
source: In the context of subcellular low-diffusive regions (Garner et al., 2023), cells may compensate for geometry-imposed constraints on packing density and size of these regions by altering the diffusivity ratio (against the bulk milieu) instead.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential cellular mechanisms.

claim: A one-parameter description relying exclusively on the average diffusion coefficient is insufficient to fully specify the dynamics in inhomogeneous diffusion.
source: To map the detailed effects of inhomogeneous diffusivity on reaction rates, however, our work suggests that a key prerequisite is to chart a suitable set of meta parameters that provide an adequate description of inhomogeneous diffusion (Jin and Verkman, 2007), as a one-parameter description relying exclusively on the average diffusion coefficient is insufficient to fully specify the dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Changes in viscosity have been shown to occur in the context of cellular processes including cell death.
source: Changes in viscosity have been shown to occur in the context of cellular processes including cell death (Kuimova et al., 2008), stress adaptation (Persson et al., 2020) and protein aggregation (Thompson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in viscosity have been shown to occur in the context of stress adaptation.
source: Changes in viscosity have been shown to occur in the context of cellular processes including cell death (Kuimova et al., 2008), stress adaptation (Persson et al., 2020) and protein aggregation (Thompson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in viscosity have been shown to occur in the context of protein aggregation.
source: Changes in viscosity have been shown to occur in the context of cellular processes including cell death (Kuimova et al., 2008), stress adaptation (Persson et al., 2020) and protein aggregation (Thompson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The effects of subcellular determinants and energy-dependent processes on how position-dependent diffusivity is maintained in a cell remains unclear.
source: The effects of all of these subcellular determinants and energy-dependent processes on how position-dependent diffusivity is maintained in a cell remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Not all cases of heterogeneous diffusivity will lead to diffusive lensing.
source: Not all cases of heterogeneous diffusivity will lead to diffusive lensing.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the phenomenon.

claim: This ambiguity is captured by the so-called Itô-Stratonovich dilemma.
source: This ambiguity is captured by the so-called Itô-Stratonovich dilemma (Lau and Lubensky, 2007; Sokolov, 2010; Tupper and Yang, 2012; Van Kampen, 1988; Volpe and Wehr, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The steady-state concentration distribution of a diffusing tracer depends not only on the localized diffusivity distribution but also on conventions based on microscopic parameters not captured in a coarse-grained model of diffusion.
source: Any mathematical conceptualization of diffusion in the presence of position-dependent diffusivity must confront this dilemma, according to which the steady-state concentration distribution of a diffusing tracer depends not only on the localized diffusivity distribution but also on conventions based on microscopic parameters not captured in a coarse-grained model of diffusion; these parameters might, for example, include correlation lengths and times of viscogens or physical characteristics of polymers (Bo et al., 2021; Kupferman et al., 2004; Lau and Lubensky, 2007; Sokolov, 2010; Tupper and Yang, 2012; Van Kampen, 1988; Vishen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Any source of heterogeneity in diffusivity can modulate diffusive lensing by means of altering either the particle or the environment-induced noise relaxation time.
source: We speculate that any source of heterogeneity in diffusivity (including, but not limited to: mesh size experienced by the diffusing tracer, temperature changes, viscogen identity, and concentration) can, in turn, modulate diffusive lensing by means of altering either the particle or the environment-induced noise relaxation time.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The Itô convention is deployed to model the nonequilibrium cellular interior.
source: While the Itô convention is deployed here to model the nonequilibrium cellular interior (Gnesotto et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2012), in some cases the isothermal convention may be better suited for modeling transport.
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations.

claim: In some cases the isothermal convention may be better suited for modeling transport.
source: While the Itô convention is deployed here to model the nonequilibrium cellular interior (Gnesotto et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2012), in some cases the isothermal convention may be better suited for modeling transport.
evidence: This is a statement about alternative modeling approaches.

claim: Diverse conventions have been used to model experimentally observed accumulation arising from varied sources of position-dependent noise.
source: Indeed, diverse conventions have been used to model experimentally observed accumulation arising from varied sources of such position-dependent noise (Bringuier, 2011; Pesce et al., 2013; Volpe and Wehr, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This work underscores the need to not only examine diffusivity distributions in vivo as a function of local composition and the environment, but also to study their time evolution in response to external stimuli.
source: Our work underscores the need to not only examine diffusivity distributions in vivo as a function of local composition and the environment, but also to study their time evolution in response to external stimuli.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the findings.

claim: Diffusive lensing serves as a potential candidate for a rudimentary mode of pre-biotic compartmentalization.
source: More speculatively, we suggest that diffusive lensing serves as a potential candidate for a rudimentary mode of pre-biotic compartmentalization.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculative.

claim: Lensing-driven accumulation of diverse biomolecules may have served to produce chemically enriched spaces, acting as an antecedent of more sophisticated, membrane-bound, and membraneless organizational modalities.
source: Lensing-driven accumulation of diverse biomolecules may have served to produce chemically enriched spaces, acting as an antecedent of more sophisticated, membrane-bound, and membraneless organizational modalities; such a protocell organization is orthogonal to currently studied models (Monnard and Walde, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about prebiotic evolution.

claim: This work demonstrates that diffusive lensing can have strong effects on transport and may be common in cellular contexts, modulating both passive and active flows.
source: This work demonstrates that diffusive lensing can have strong effects on transport and may be common in cellular contexts, modulating both passive and active flows.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the work's findings.

claim: Agent-based modeling of diffusion was conducted via 2D random walk simulations.
source: Agent-based modeling of diffusion was conducted via 2D random walk simulations.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used.

claim: The underlying diffusion equations contain additive, separable contributions from each dimension, and this extends to 3D as well.
source: Irrespective of how the Itô-Stratonovich dilemma is interrogated, the underlying diffusion equations contain additive, separable contributions from each dimension, and this extends to 3D as well.
evidence: This is a statement about the mathematical properties of diffusion equations.

claim: Calculations were carried out in 2D for simplicity and visualizability.
source: Calculations were, therefore, carried out in 2D for simplicity and visualizability.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological choice.

claim: Non-interacting point particles were initialized uniformly in a 2D simulation region with an aspect ratio matching that of an E. coli bacterium.
source: Non-interacting point particles were initialized uniformly in a 2D simulation region with an aspect ratio matching that of an E. coli bacterium (Phillips et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup.

claim: Across a large number of steps, the distribution of displacements converges to the normal distribution by virtue of the central limit theorem.
source: Across a large number of steps, the distribution of displacements converges to the normal distribution by virtue of the central limit theorem.
evidence: This is a statement about the mathematical properties of the simulation.

claim: The diffusion coefficient was arrived at as an emergent property of trajectories comprising a simulation, in a ground-up fashion.
source: While sampling was not performed via the normal distribution directly by using the diffusion coefficient (D) as a parameter, the diffusion coefficient was instead arrived at as an emergent property of trajectories comprising a simulation, in a ground-up fashion.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: At all times, step sizes were sampled from distributions defined by the diffusivity around the present position in accordance with the Itô interpretation of multiplicative noise.
source: At all times, step sizes were sampled from distributions defined by the diffusivity around the present position in accordance with the Itô interpretation of multiplicative noise (Volpe and Wehr, 2016) (for theoretical predictions of the steady-state behaviors, see Numerical methods for the diffusion equations).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation algorithm and its theoretical basis.

claim: In the simulations which included inter-particle interactions, these interactions were modeled via a neighbor-sensing approach.
source: In the simulations which included inter-particle interactions, these interactions were modeled via a neighbor-sensing approach.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation method.

claim: Such a rule-based approach modeled an effective attractive potential for the inter-particle interactions.
source: Such a rule-based approach modeled an effective attractive potential for the inter-particle interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the interaction model.

claim: No two disks were allowed to overlap and all disks were kept confined within the boundaries of the simulation region.
source: No two disks were allowed to overlap and all disks were kept confined within the boundaries of the simulation region.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation constraints.

claim: Analysis of particle trajectories was carried out via quantifying the mean squared displacements (MSD).
source: Analysis of particle trajectories was carried out via quantifying the mean squared displacements (MSD).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: These MSDs were calculated from 10^4 trajectories (each 10^5 timesteps in duration) per simulation.
source: These were calculated from 104 trajectories (each 105 timesteps in duration) per simulation.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis parameters.

claim: In silico FRAP studies were performed on the diffusion simulations to quantify emergent dynamics at the mesoscale.
source: In silico fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) studies were performed on the diffusion simulations to quantify emergent dynamics at the mesoscale.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: 10^5 particles were deployed for a total duration of 0.5 s (10^4 epochs) in the in silico FRAP simulations.
source: 105 particles were deployed for a total duration of 0.5 s (104 epochs).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation parameters.

claim: Circular regions (radius of 0.2 μm) were chosen as the regions of interest (ROIs) in the in silico FRAP simulations.
source: Circular regions (radius of 0.2 μm) were chosen as the regions of interest (ROIs).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation setup.

claim: In silico photobleaching was instantaneously performed and involved assigning the particles in the ROI the photobleach status.
source: In silico photobleaching was instantaneously performed and involved assigning the particles in the ROI the photobleach status.
